name: Centrism
summary: Centrism takes an intermediate, pragmatic position between left and right, preferring moderate policy and practical results to ideological appeals. Its best-documented programmes, the Third Way or New Centre of Blair, Schroeder and the US New Democrats and the radical middle of Satin and of Halstead and Lind, accept a market economy and an active but modernised state, pair rights with responsibilities and favour opportunity over equal outcomes. On most other questions its sources record no common position.
scope: The reference works define centrism as a relational, intermediate and pragmatic position between left and right (s5, s6). This profile reads it through the programmes those works and the Third Way literature tie to it: the Blair-Schroeder Third Way / New Centre paper (1999), the New Democrat agenda as Clinton restated it (the 1990 New Orleans Declaration, 1995 and 2000 remarks), and the radical-middle texts (Satin; Halstead and Lind as reported). It excludes centrist parties as such, centrist populism, and agrarian or Christian-democratic centres, none of which the sources describe as part of the ideology. Where the strands differ (pensions, for example) the answer is mixed.

notes: Radical-middle texts (Satin; Halstead and Lind as reviewed) are used only where they state a position; Third Way and New Democrat texts carry most answers. Themes searched: economy and taxes, welfare and work, public finance, trade and globalisation, Europe and world affairs, crime, race and civil rights, environment, family, democracy and government, force and conscription, using the Third Way and New Democrat primary texts, the radical-middle texts and the scholarship on them. The sources say little on religion, sex and gender, courts and constitutions, nationalism, technology and animals; those stay null. The two strands differ on pensions and taxes; Satin and Halstead and Lind are the radical middle's own accounts and Kahlenberg's and Satin's reviews report Halstead and Lind's proposals. Britannica and Merriam-Webster refused scripted access and were not used. Giddens's The Third Way (1998) and Halstead and Lind's The Radical Center (2001) were not available as text, so they are cited only through reviews.
